name: Dogfight Position
description: Master the Dogfight position in BJJ half guard. Dynamic kneeling position with 75% sweep success at advanced levels. Complete guide to underhook battles, back takes, and sweeps.
variant_uniqueness: Elevated kneeling posture for explosive access
overview:
**Dogfight Position** (also called Dogfight Half Guard or Underhook Battle Position) is a dynamic half guard variation where both practitioners are up on their knees facing each other in a competitive underhook battle. This elevated kneeling configuration creates high-action scrambling scenarios that define modern half guard competition at the highest levels. Success rate: Beginner 45% retention, Advanced 75% retention. Requires: underhook establishment, active frames, constant forward pressure.

The name "dogfight" comes from the scrambling, competitive nature where both players aggressively vie for dominant grips and positioning like dogs fighting - a perfect description of the chaotic, highly dynamic exchanges that occur. Unlike flat [[Half Guard]] where the bottom player is on their back, **Dogfight Position** has both practitioners elevated on their knees creating equal offensive opportunities and rapid position changes. The bottom player has established an underhook from flat half guard and elevated to their knees, while the top player fights to maintain passing pressure through [[Whizzer Control|whizzer]] and crossface attempts.

From **Dogfight Position**, you have multiple high-percentage attacks: [[Old School Sweep]] (70% advanced success), [[Back Take Generic|back takes]] (65% advanced), and [[Deep Half Entry|deep half transitions]] (75% advanced). The position is neutral-to-slightly-advantageous for the player with the deeper underhook, offering numerous pathways to sweeps, back control, and position improvements. This elevated posture creates dynamic movements and rarely remains static - exchanges typically resolve within 30-90 seconds to sweeps, back takes, or passes.

The position is favored in modern no-gi grappling and has become a cornerstone of competitive half guard systems. Works in both gi and no-gi, though no-gi creates faster scrambles due to lack of gripping controls. **Dogfight Position** rewards aggressive, forward-moving practitioners who chain multiple techniques together and capitalize on opponent's balance disruptions while maintaining superior underhook control.
state_invariants: Both practitioners are elevated on their knees in upright or semi-upright kneeling positions, with weight distributed through knees and posting points, creating an inherently unstable equilibrium where small adjustments determine positional outcomes

Active underhook battle occurring with at least one player having established underhook control around opponent's torso, ideally reaching to the far shoulder, while the opponent typically counters with whizzer (overhook) control pulling back and downward
Bottom player's inside leg remains trapped between top player's thighs in half guard configuration, though the elevated posture creates space and mobility compared to flat half guard positions

Both players' upper bodies are relatively upright and face-to-face or slightly angled, with heads in close proximity fighting for superior positioning, preventing either player from achieving fully dominant control

Dynamic tension maintained through the underhook/whizzer battle with both players using frames (knee shields, butterfly hooks, posting hands) to manage distance and create or deny offensive opportunities
Position characterized by constant movement and weight distribution changes rather than static control, with both players actively fighting to advance their position or prevent opponent advancement

step_by_step: From flat [[Half Guard]] bottom position, establish deep underhook on one side reaching to opponent's far shoulder
Create initial space by using your outside leg as knee shield or butterfly hook to prevent opponent's chest pressure
Bridge your hips off the mat while driving forward pressure through your underhook, initiating elevation
Bring your inside knee (trapped leg side) underneath your body while maintaining underhook connection
Post your outside leg for base stability, keeping it close to your body rather than extended far out
Drive your head high and forward into opponent's chest, using it as additional pressure point and control
Complete elevation by coming fully to your knees in upright kneeling posture facing opponent
Immediately establish active frames with your outside leg (knee shield or butterfly hook) to prevent being flattened
Maintain constant forward pressure through underhook - never pull backward or create separation voluntarily
Begin chaining offensive attacks (sweeps, back takes, transitions) immediately upon reaching Dogfight configuration
how_to_enter.key_details: The entry from flat half guard to Dogfight is critical - you must elevate explosively while maintaining your underhook throughout. If you lose the underhook during elevation, opponent will flatten you immediately. Time your elevation when opponent is not applying maximum pressure. Success rate: Beginner 40%, Intermediate 60%, Advanced 75%.

prerequisites: Understanding of [[Half Guard]] bottom mechanics and frame creation principles
Ability to establish and maintain deep underhook control under pressure
Hip mobility to elevate from flat position to kneeling posture while maintaining leg entanglement
Active frame maintenance using knee shield, butterfly hooks, or posted legs to manage distance
Understanding of forward pressure mechanics and when to drive versus when to create space
Grip fighting fundamentals to compete for dominant inside positioning against whizzer attempts
key_principles: Maintain constant forward pressure through the underhook, driving into opponent to prevent them from establishing stable base and controlling the direction of engagement
Use active frames (knee shield, butterfly hook, posted leg) to create and maintain space, preventing opponent from closing distance and flattening you to the mat
Keep your head level with or higher than opponent's head to control upper body battles and prevent being driven backward or flattened
Chain multiple techniques together without pausing—if one attack is defended, immediately flow to alternate sweep, back take, or position improvement based on opponent's defensive reactions
Fight aggressively for the underhook battle as the primary control point, understanding that losing the underhook typically results in being flattened and losing offensive momentum
Stay active and mobile with constant weight shifts and directional changes—Dogfight rewards dynamic movement over static holding and creates reactions to capitalize on
Control opponent's far hip or near-side hip with free hand to limit their mobility and posting options while setting up sweeps and transitions

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent attempts to flatten you with crossface or removes their whizzer, exposing their back
Opponent drives forward pressure, attempts to smash pass, or posts their free leg far out creating space underneath
Opponent posts their far leg to prevent back take or establishes strong base with outside leg
Opponent shifts weight backward to counter underhook pressure or creates vertical posture
Opponent establishes dominant whizzer and you cannot maintain upright posture against pressure

decision_tree.condition: If opponent has strong whizzer and is driving you backward with heavy crossface pressure
If opponent's far leg is posted wide and vulnerable to being controlled
If opponent loses whizzer control, exposes their back, or commits weight forward excessively
If opponent maintains upright posture and posts their free leg far out for base
If opponent attempts to circle their trapped leg free while maintaining balance

common_errors.error: Allowing the top player to flatten you to the mat by not maintaining active frames and forward pressure
common_errors.consequence: Loss of all offensive opportunities and transition to defensive flat half guard where sweeps become significantly more difficult and energy-intensive
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant forward pressure with your underhook while keeping your knee shield or butterfly hook actively pushing to prevent being driven backward—never voluntarily move backward or allow frames to collapse

common_errors.error: Staying static in the Dogfight position without chaining techniques or creating constant pressure changes
common_errors.consequence: The top player establishes strong grips and controls, eventually passing or flattening you as they solve the static puzzle through superior positioning
common_errors.correction: Constantly flow between sweep attempts, back take entries, and position improvements—if one attack is defended, immediately chain to the next without pausing or resetting to starting position

common_errors.error: Losing the underhook battle by allowing opponent to strip it or failing to fight for deep underhook positioning
common_errors.consequence: Without the underhook as your primary offensive tool, the top player can easily flatten and pass your guard using crossface and shoulder pressure
common_errors.correction: Fight aggressively for the underhook and never give it up voluntarily—if you lose it, immediately work to recover it or transition to deep half or other defensive positions

common_errors.error: Allowing your head to drop below the opponent's head level or keeping it too far from their body
common_errors.consequence: The top player can drive forward pressure and flatten you to the mat, eliminating your upright posture and all offensive capabilities
common_errors.correction: Keep your head high and pressed against opponent's body by driving forward with your underhook—use your head as an additional control point and pressure source

common_errors.error: Not controlling the opponent's far hip or leg when attempting sweeps, allowing them to post and base out
common_errors.consequence: The opponent easily defends all sweep attempts by posting their free leg, potentially countering with passes as you overextend on failed sweeps
common_errors.correction: When executing sweeps like the Old School, ensure you control the opponent's far leg or hip with your free hand to prevent posting and maximize sweep success

common_errors.error: Giving up space by pulling backward instead of maintaining constant forward driving pressure
common_errors.consequence: Creates distance that allows the top player to establish better grips, improve their base, and launch passing attacks without resistance
common_errors.correction: Constantly drive forward with your underhook and upper body while using your frames to manage optimal distance—never voluntarily create separation

common_errors.error: Posting your outside leg too far away from your body, reducing your ability to generate power and change angles
common_errors.consequence: Loss of mobility and sweep power, making it easy for opponent to circle around your posted leg or drive through your weakened base
common_errors.correction: Keep your outside posting leg relatively close to your body with knee and foot ready to drive or reposition quickly, maintaining compact base that generates power in multiple directions

training_drills.name: Dogfight Position Retention Drill
training_drills.description: Partner starts in Dogfight with training partner applying progressive resistance to flatten them or strip the underhook. Bottom player maintains upright posture for 2-minute rounds while defending flattening attempts through active frames, forward underhook pressure, and superior head position. Partner gradually increases pressure intensity from 50% to 75% to 100% across multiple rounds. Focus on constant movement and base maintenance.

training_drills.name: Sweep Chain Flow Drill
training_drills.description: From Dogfight position, bottom player practices chaining together Old School sweep to John Wayne sweep to Waiter sweep to Deep Half entry in continuous sequence. Top player provides realistic progressive defense to first technique, forcing smooth transitions to second and third options without resetting to starting position. Emphasizes reading opponent's defensive reactions and flowing between techniques based on their weight distribution and posting patterns.

training_drills.name: Back Take vs Sweep Decision Drill
training_drills.description: Start in Dogfight with top partner randomly choosing to defend either back take (by keeping hips low and whizzer tight) or sweep (by posting wide and maintaining vertical base). Bottom player practices reading defensive posture through tactile feedback and selecting appropriate attack based on opponent's positioning. Develop sensitivity to when back is exposed versus when legs are vulnerable to sweeps.

training_drills.name: Underhook Battle Positional Sparring
training_drills.description: Begin in Dogfight with both players competing for underhook advantage and superior positioning. First player to secure dominant underhook and maintain it for 5 seconds wins that exchange. Then transition to full Dogfight sparring where bottom player attempts sweeps/back takes while top player attempts to pass or flatten. Reset to neutral Dogfight every 90 seconds. Track success rates to identify weaknesses.

training_drills.name: Dogfight Entry Progression Drill
training_drills.description: Practice entering Dogfight from flat half guard bottom with progressive resistance. Partner starts passive, then adds increasing resistance with whizzer and crossface pressure. Focus on establishing deep underhook, coming to knees with proper base, and maintaining head position while creating frames. Chain directly into sweep or back take attempts from successful entries.

position_metrics.average_time: 30-90 seconds before transition to sweep, back take, or pass occurs (highly dynamic position with rapid resolution)

comparison_with_related_positions.dogfight_vs_deep_half: **When to use Dogfight:** When you have space to elevate, want aggressive back take opportunities, and opponent is not applying crushing forward pressure. **When to use [[Deep Half Guard]]:** When opponent drives heavy forward pressure, you need defensive depth, or they post wide making deep half entry available. **Key difference:** Dogfight is elevated and aggressive (65% back take success advanced), while Deep Half is low and defensive with different sweep mechanics. Both work from [[Half Guard]] but serve different strategic purposes.
comparison_with_related_positions.dogfight_vs_flat_half_guard: **Dogfight Position** = Both players on knees, upright posture, equal offensive access, highly dynamic scrambles. **[[Half Guard]]** (flat) = Bottom player on back, top player has gravity advantage, bottom player more defensive. **Elevation advantage:** In Dogfight you create more equal weight distribution (45% beginner retention vs 35% in flat half), generate significantly more sweeping force, and create better angles for back takes. Dogfight is the offensive evolution of flat half guard.
comparison_with_related_positions.dogfight_vs_butterfly_guard: Both involve underhook battles and elevated postures, but **[[Butterfly Guard]]** has both legs free for hooks while **Dogfight Position** has one leg trapped in half guard configuration. Dogfight offers more control through leg entanglement but less mobility. Butterfly specializes in elevation sweeps; Dogfight specializes in back takes and old school sweeps. Strategic choice depends on whether you want mobility (Butterfly) or control (Dogfight).
comparison_with_related_positions.gi_vs_no_gi_differences: **No-gi Dogfight:** Faster scrambles, more explosive movements, underhook battle more critical since no collar grips available. Transitions happen more rapidly (average 30-60 seconds). **Gi Dogfight:** Slower pace with collar and sleeve grips controlling tempo, more opportunities for grip fighting strategies, easier to maintain position longer (60-90 seconds average). Both effective but no-gi rewards athletic explosiveness while gi rewards technical grip mastery. 10th Planet system developed Dogfight primarily for no-gi competition.

skill_level_guide.is_dogfight_good_for_beginners: **Challenging but valuable for beginners** (45% retention rate). The underhook battles and frame maintenance teach essential half guard concepts. **Start here:** Master flat [[Half Guard]] first, develop underhook control, practice elevation drills without resistance. **Beginner focus:** Defensive retention and underhook maintenance rather than advanced sweeps. **Success timeline:** Expect 6-12 months to develop comfortable Dogfight game. Position retention improves significantly with experience: Beginner 45% → Intermediate 60% → Advanced 75%.
skill_level_guide.intermediate_development: At intermediate level (60% retention rate), focus on chaining techniques together rather than single attacks. **Key development areas:** Combine [[Old School Sweep]] with [[Back Take Generic]] threats (55% and 50% success), develop sensitivity to opponent weight distribution, improve transition speed to [[Deep Half Guard]] (60% success). Training emphasis: Positional sparring, timing drills, decision-tree development.
skill_level_guide.advanced_mastery: Advanced practitioners (75% retention rate) use Dogfight as offensive launching platform with high success rates across all techniques. **Advanced skills:** Instant recognition of sweep vs back take opportunities (70% and 65% success), seamless chains between multiple attacks, ability to create reactions through feints, expert-level grip fighting. **Competition application:** At black belt level, threat of back take often more valuable than actual back take - forces defensive postures that open sweep opportunities.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What are the best sweeps from Dogfight Position?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The highest percentage sweeps from **Dogfight Position** are: [[Old School Sweep]] (70% advanced success) when opponent posts far leg wide, [[Deep Half Entry]] (75% advanced) when opponent drives forward, and [[Underhook Sweep from Half]] (65% advanced) when opponent loses whizzer control. For beginners, focus on Old School sweep (40% success) as it's the most fundamental. Chain these together - if Old School is defended, immediately switch to back take or deep half based on opponent's reaction.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How do you maintain the underhook in Dogfight?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Maintain the underhook by: (1) Driving constant forward pressure into opponent - never pull backward, (2) Keep your head high level with or above opponent's head, (3) Connect your underhook hand to your own hip or opponent's far shoulder for maximum depth, (4) If opponent strips underhook, immediately re-establish or transition to [[Deep Half Guard]] or [[Rolling to Guard|closed guard recovery]]. **Critical principle:** Losing the underhook typically means being flattened and losing all offensive momentum - fight aggressively to never give it up voluntarily.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What submissions can you finish from Dogfight?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Direct submissions: [[Electric Chair Submission]] (50% advanced success) via lockdown mechanics. **High-percentage submission paths:** Dogfight → [[Back Take Generic|Back Control]] → [[Rear Naked Choke]] (most common), Dogfight → [[Old School Sweep]] → [[Mount]] → [[Armbar from Mount]], or Dogfight → [[Deep Half Entry|Deep Half]] → [[Waiter Sweep]] → Mount → [[Kimura from Mount]]. Most submissions come after position advancement rather than directly from Dogfight itself.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How long can you stay in Dogfight Position?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: **Dogfight Position** typically lasts 30-90 seconds before resolving to sweep, back take, or pass due to its highly dynamic nature. The position is inherently unstable with both players actively fighting for advancement - staying static longer than 90 seconds usually means one player isn't attacking aggressively enough. **Competition context:** In tournaments, expect rapid position changes. Use Dogfight as launching platform for immediate attacks rather than position to maintain long-term.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is Dogfight Position better in gi or no-gi?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: **Dogfight Position** works in both gi and no-gi but is especially dynamic in no-gi where lack of gi grips creates faster scrambles and more explosive exchanges. **No-gi advantages:** Faster transitions, more athletic movement, underhook battle paramount. **Gi advantages:** More grip fighting options, easier to control pace, collar and sleeve grips add control layers. The position was refined in modern no-gi competition (Gordon Ryan, Craig Jones) but remains effective in gi. 10th Planet system developed extensive Dogfight variations specifically for no-gi application.

frequently_asked_questions.question: When should you use Dogfight instead of Deep Half Guard?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: **Use Dogfight when:** You have space to elevate, want aggressive back take opportunities (65% advanced vs 40% from Deep Half), opponent is upright not applying crushing pressure, you favor dynamic scrambling. **Use [[Deep Half Guard]] when:** Opponent drives heavy forward pressure making elevation impossible, you need defensive depth and recovery time, opponent posts wide creating deep half entry opportunity, you want high-percentage sweep mechanics (75% Waiter sweep advanced). Strategic choice: Dogfight = aggressive/offensive, Deep Half = defensive/technical.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What does Gordon Ryan say about Dogfight Position?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Gordon Ryan: "Dogfight is one of my favorite half guard positions in competition because it's inherently aggressive and puts the top player in a defensive mindset. I'm always threatening the back take first, which forces opponents to defend with whizzer, and when they defend the back aggressively, the [[Old School Sweep]] becomes available. At high levels, you absolutely cannot stay static - you must immediately attack with commitment or you'll get passed. The threat of the back take is often more valuable than the actual back take itself, forcing them into defensive postures that make them vulnerable to sweeps."

expert_insights.danaher: The **Dogfight Position** represents a critical inflection point in the half guard game where biomechanical advantage is determined entirely by superior control of the underhook battle and understanding of weight distribution principles. The position's effectiveness stems from the bottom player's ability to elevate their center of gravity while maintaining a strong connection through the underhook, which creates multiple sweeping vectors and back exposure opportunities that are mechanically superior to flat [[Half Guard]] configurations. The key biomechanical principle is that by coming up to your knees, you've created a more equal weight distribution compared to flat half guard, which allows you to generate significantly more force in your sweeping and advancing movements while simultaneously creating instability in your opponent's base. The underhook becomes your primary steering mechanism - by driving it forward and upward with proper hip connection, you can manipulate your opponent's base and create the angle necessary for [[Back Take Generic|back takes]] or leg attacks. The position demands constant activity because any static moment allows the top player to solve the puzzle through superior gripping and pressure application, consolidating their base and initiating passing sequences. I teach my students to view **Dogfight** not as a position to maintain, but as a launching platform for immediate advancement to either [[Back Control|the back]] or a superior top position through systematic chaining of techniques based on opponent's defensive reactions.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: **Dogfight** is one of my favorite half guard positions in competition because it's inherently aggressive and puts the top player in a defensive mindset where they're reacting to my attacks rather than imposing their passing game. From this position, I'm always threatening the [[Back Take Generic|back take]] first and foremost, which forces my opponent to defend with their whizzer and keep their hips low, and when they defend the back aggressively, the [[Old School Sweep]] becomes available because they've committed their base in one direction. The key competitive insight is understanding that at high levels, you absolutely cannot stay static in Dogfight - you must immediately attack with commitment or you'll get passed by opponents who understand the position. I chain together back take attempts with the Old School sweep constantly in competition, and if both are defended effectively, I drop to [[Deep Half Guard|deep half]] and start the entire sequence again from a different angle. The position rewards aggressive, forward-moving grapplers who aren't afraid to commit to their attacks and accept some risk of being countered. Against elite opponents, I've found that the threat of the back take is often more valuable than the actual back take itself, because it forces them into defensive postures with poor base that make them extremely vulnerable to sweeps and position advancements. In no-gi competition especially, this position is even more dynamic because without the gi grips to slow things down, you can really explode into your attacks and catch opponents off guard with the speed and commitment of your transitions between techniques.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The **Dogfight**, which we call the '[[Electric Chair]] position' or '93 Guard' in the 10th Planet system, is where the [[Lockdown]] game gets really interesting and opens up our entire half guard offensive system. While traditional BJJ focuses primarily on the underhook battle and [[Old School Sweep]] from here, we've developed an entire subsystem around the lockdown and whip-up mechanics that create unique sweeping and submission opportunities that most competitors don't anticipate. The beauty of Dogfight is that it's a position of constant motion and creativity - there's no single 'correct' way to attack from here, which means you can develop your own personal style and combinations that work with your body type and athletic attributes. I teach students to use the Dogfight as both an offensive launching platform and a recovery position when they need to catch their breath in half guard because you're much harder to flatten and control when you're up on your knees with proper frames. From here, you can hit the Electric Chair sweep, whip up to the [[Truck]] position for [[Twister]] attacks, or if you're feeling creative, go for the [[Vaporizer]] submission. The key innovation we brought to this position is understanding that you don't always need the traditional underhook to be successful - sometimes the lockdown itself provides enough control to sweep and advance, especially if you understand the biomechanics of stretching your opponent out and creating angles that compromise their base. This position perfectly embodies the 10th Planet philosophy of turning traditionally defensive positions into aggressive, submission-hunting platforms where you're always threatening to finish the match rather than just survive and advance position.
